claims.text: Two-phase coexistence or interface-pinning simulations can be used to predict melting properties of refractory materials.
Advanced sampling methods such as metadynamics or nested sampling can enhance the proposed melting simulations.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on DFT data can be used in place of direct ab initio molecular dynamics in the proposed protocol.
The simulations are performed near the melting point under conditions where solid and liquid coexist.
A maintained solid-liquid interface mediates the free-energy difference between the solid and liquid phases.
Advanced sampling efficiently maps the free-energy landscape across the solid-liquid interface.
Advanced sampling captures the key thermodynamic transitions relevant to melting.
DFT-trained machine-learned potentials provide an accurate representation of interatomic forces.
DFT-trained machine-learned potentials are computationally more efficient than direct DFT-based thermodynamic integration with ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method can determine melting temperature.
The proposed method can determine entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
The proposed method can determine the volume change at melting.
The predicted melting properties will agree within roughly 10% of full ab initio results.
The proposed method will drastically reduce computational cost relative to full DFT-based thermodynamic integration.
The accuracy and computational savings depend on the quality of the machine-learned potential and material-specific thermodynamics.
The method's accuracy may be uncertain for materials with strong anharmonic effects or significant quantum nuclear effects.
